q: A 74-year-old man presents 90 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and inability to speak. On examination he has a dense right hemiplegia affecting face, arm and leg equally, a right homonymous hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction with global aphasia and neglect. Blood pressure is 176/94 mmHg and capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. An urgent non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. He was independent at baseline. Using the Oxford (Bamford) classification, how is this stroke best categorised?
options: Total anterior circulation syndrome (TACS)
Partial anterior circulation syndrome (PACS)
Lacunar syndrome (LACS)
Posterior circulation syndrome (POCS)
Pure motor lacunar stroke
explain: The Bamford/Oxford Community Stroke Project (OCSP) classification is clinical and requires all three of: (1) higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect); (2) homonymous hemianopia; (3) motor and/or sensory deficit of at least two of face, arm, leg. 🧠 This man has all three — global aphasia + neglect, homonymous hemianopia, and a dense hemiplegia of face/arm/leg — so this is a TACS, implying occlusion of the proximal MCA or ICA. TACS carries the worst prognosis (~60% dead at one year, only ~5% independent). A PACS has only two of the three components (or higher cortical dysfunction alone). A LACS has no cortical signs or hemianopia (e.g. pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis). A POCS features cranial nerve palsies with contralateral tract signs, cerebellar signs, or isolated hemianopia. Recognising a TACS should trigger urgent consideration of thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

A POCS features cranial nerve palsies with contralateral tract signs, cerebellar signs, or isolated hemianopia. Recognising a TACS should trigger urgent consideration of thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

This defines a total anterior circulation syndrome, implicating proximal MCA/ICA occlusion and carrying the worst functional prognosis.

B.html: A PACS requires only two of the three TACS components, or isolated higher cortical dysfunction. This patient fulfils all three criteria, so the syndrome is total rather than partial.

C.html: Lacunar syndromes arise from small perforator disease and by definition lack cortical signs and hemianopia. The presence of aphasia, neglect and a visual field defect excludes a lacunar stroke.

D.html: Posterior circulation syndromes typically feature brainstem/cerebellar signs, crossed deficits or isolated hemianopia. The dominant cortical language and neglect signs point firmly to the anterior circulation.

E.html: Pure motor stroke is a lacunar subtype confined to weakness without cortical features. Global aphasia, neglect and hemianopia are cortical and incompatible with this category.

q: A 32-year-old woman is referred with a subacute painful loss of vision in the right eye over several days, now recovering. Two years ago she had transient numbness and tingling of both legs lasting three weeks that resolved. Examination shows a right relative afferent pupillary defect and mild right optic disc pallor; the remainder is normal. MRI of the brain and whole spine demonstrates several periventricular and one juxtacortical T2 lesion, plus an asymptomatic enhancing cervical cord lesion alongside a non-enhancing thoracic lesion. CSF shows unmatched oligoclonal bands. According to the 2017 McDonald criteria, which single feature best establishes the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis here?
options: The relative afferent pupillary defect confirming optic neuritis
The presence of optic disc pallor indicating a prior attack
Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions demonstrating dissemination in time
A single juxtacortical lesion demonstrating dissemination in space
Elevated CSF protein above 0.45 g/L
explain: The 2017 McDonald criteria require dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT). DIS = ≥1 T2 lesion in ≥2 of four CNS regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord). DIT = either a new lesion on follow-up, or simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single scan, or substitution by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. ⏱️ Here, DIS is already satisfied (periventricular, juxtacortical and cord). The single feature that establishes DIT is the co-existence of an enhancing cervical lesion with a non-enhancing thoracic lesion on the same scan — lesions of different ages. The RAPD and disc pallor are clinical signs of optic neuritis but do not by themselves prove dissemination. Unmatched oligoclonal bands can substitute for DIT under the 2017 revision, but the question asks for the feature demonstrated by these findings, and simultaneous enhancing/non-enhancing lesions are the classic radiological proof. CSF protein elevation is non-specific and not a criterion.

CSF protein elevation is non-specific and not a criterion.

B.html: Disc pallor implies a previous optic nerve insult but does not fulfil the radiological or CSF requirements for dissemination in time. The optic nerve is not currently counted among the four DIS regions in routine 2017 criteria.

D.html: A juxtacortical lesion contributes to dissemination in space, not time. Dissemination in space is already satisfied here; the outstanding requirement is dissemination in time.

E.html: A raised CSF protein is non-specific and is not part of the McDonald criteria. It is the presence of CSF-specific (unmatched) oligoclonal bands, not protein level, that can substitute for dissemination in time.

q: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department having had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure witnessed by paramedics. On arrival he is still convulsing and has now been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. Airway is patent with high-flow oxygen applied, capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L and he has good intravenous access. He takes lamotrigine for known epilepsy but recently ran out. According to current UK (NICE/ABN) guidance for convulsing status epilepticus, what is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological step?
options: Load with intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg immediately
Intravenous lorazepam 4 mg
Rectal diazepam 10 mg
Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg
Rapid-sequence induction with propofol and intubation
explain: Convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting ≥5 minutes (or repeated seizures without recovery). The first-line treatment when IV access is available is a benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg), repeated once after 5–10 minutes if seizures continue. ⚡ Where there is no IV access, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam is used — but this patient has good access, so IV lorazepam is preferred over rectal diazepam. If seizures persist after two doses of benzodiazepine, second-line agents (IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate) are given — the ESETT trial showed these three are broadly equivalent in efficacy. Phenytoin loading and levetiracetam are therefore second-line, not the immediate step. General anaesthesia with intubation (propofol, thiopental) is reserved for refractory status persisting beyond second-line therapy, typically at 30+ minutes, and requires ICU. Always correct hypoglycaemia and give parenteral thiamine if alcohol/malnutrition is suspected; glucose here is normal.

q: A 68-year-old woman is referred with a two-year history of progressive slowness. Her family note a stooped, shuffling gait and reduced facial expression. On examination there is a 4–6 Hz rest tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia that is markedly asymmetrical, worse on the right. Eye movements are full, blood pressure shows no significant postural drop, and there is no early cognitive impairment or hallucination. Her symptoms improve substantially when levodopa is introduced. Which single pathological mechanism best explains the core motor features in this patient?
options: Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies
Deposition of tau in a 4-repeat isoform within midbrain and basal ganglia
Autoimmune blockade of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Depletion of striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurones
Widespread demyelination of central white matter tracts
explain: This is classic idiopathic Parkinson's disease: asymmetrical onset, a 4–6 Hz rest ("pill-rolling") tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a good, sustained response to levodopa, without early red flags for a Parkinson-plus syndrome. 🧠 The underlying mechanism is progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta, whose axons project to the striatum. Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine disinhibits the indirect pathway and reduces facilitation of the direct pathway, producing the hypokinetic features. The pathological hallmark is intracytoplasmic alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies). 4-repeat tau deposition characterises progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration (which respond poorly to levodopa and show early falls, vertical gaze palsy, or apraxia). Postsynaptic ACh-receptor blockade is myasthenia gravis. Striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurone loss causes Huntington's chorea. Central demyelination describes multiple sclerosis. The excellent levodopa response strongly favours a dopaminergic, synucleinopathic process rather than a tauopathy.

C.html: Autoimmune blockade of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors is the mechanism of myasthenia gravis, causing fatigable weakness and ptosis, not rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia. It does not respond to levodopa.

q: A 58-year-old man presents with a three-month history of double vision and drooping eyelids that are worse in the evening and after reading. He also describes difficulty chewing towards the end of a meal and a nasal quality to his speech. Examination confirms fatigable ptosis and complex ophthalmoparesis; power is initially normal but declines on sustained effort. Reflexes are preserved and there is no autonomic dysfunction. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and CT of the thorax is requested. Which single investigation finding would most strongly support the underlying diagnosis by demonstrating the electrophysiological hallmark of this condition?
options: Incremental response of >100% on high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation
Decremental response of >10% on low-frequency (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation
Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves at rest
Conduction block with prolonged distal motor latencies
Myotonic discharges with a 'dive-bomber' sound on EMG
explain: The picture — fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar weakness worse with sustained effort, positive ACh-receptor antibodies, and preserved reflexes/autonomic function — is myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated attack on postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction. 🔌 Because receptors are depleted, repeated nerve stimulation progressively exhausts the safety margin of transmission. On low-frequency (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation this produces a characteristic decremental response (>10%) in compound muscle action potential amplitude. Single-fibre EMG showing increased jitter is even more sensitive. An incremental response on high-frequency stimulation is the hallmark of the presynaptic Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies, often with small-cell lung cancer, and areflexia that improves with exercise). Fibrillations/positive sharp waves indicate denervation. Conduction block with prolonged latencies suggests an acquired demyelinating neuropathy (e.g. GBS/CIDP). Myotonic 'dive-bomber' discharges occur in myotonic dystrophy. Thoracic CT is performed to detect a thymoma.

On low-frequency (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation this produces a characteristic decremental response (>10%) in compound muscle action potential amplitude. Myotonic 'dive-bomber' discharges occur in myotonic dystrophy. Thoracic CT is performed to detect a thymoma.

B.html: Correct. In myasthenia gravis, postsynaptic ACh-receptor depletion narrows the safety margin of transmission, so low-frequency (3 Hz) repetitive stimulation produces a decremental CMAP response of over 10%. This is the classic electrophysiological hallmark of the disorder.

q: A 45-year-old man is admitted with ascending symmetrical weakness of both legs progressing over five days to involve the arms, following an episode of bloody diarrhoea three weeks earlier. Examination shows a flaccid tetraparesis with globally absent reflexes and mild distal sensory loss; there is bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness. He is short of breath. Forced vital capacity has fallen from 3.2 L to 1.4 L over six hours. Blood pressure fluctuates between 90/50 and 190/100 mmHg. Nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating pattern. Which single feature most urgently mandates transfer to a critical care environment?
options: Bilateral facial weakness
Globally absent deep tendon reflexes
Antecedent Campylobacter jejuni diarrhoea
A forced vital capacity of 1.4 L that is falling rapidly
Demyelinating changes on nerve conduction studies
explain: This is Guillain–Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy), classically post-Campylobacter jejuni, with ascending flaccid areflexic weakness, cytoalbuminological dissociation in CSF, and molecular mimicry driving anti-ganglioside antibodies. ⚠️ The most immediately life-threatening complication is neuromuscular respiratory failure. A forced vital capacity that is low (≤1.5 L or ~15–20 mL/kg) and falling rapidly predicts imminent need for ventilatory support; the '20/30/40 rule' (FVC <20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure < −30, maximal expiratory pressure < +40 cmH₂O) flags impending failure. This must trigger critical care transfer for monitoring and elective intubation before a crisis — arterial oxygen desaturation is a late sign. The fluctuating blood pressure signals autonomic instability, another reason for close monitoring. Facial weakness, areflexia, the antecedent infection and the demyelinating NCS all support the diagnosis but do not themselves demand ICU. Treatment is IVIg or plasma exchange (equally effective); steroids are not beneficial in GBS.

q: A 62-year-old man presents with an 8-month history of progressive weakness. He has wasting and fasciculations of the hands and tongue, with brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses in the legs despite marked distal wasting. There is no sensory loss, no sphincter disturbance and eye movements are normal. Speech is dysarthric and he has occasional choking on liquids. Cognition is largely preserved. Nerve conduction studies are normal, and needle EMG shows widespread fibrillations and fasciculations with large-amplitude motor units. Which single feature is most characteristic of the underlying diagnosis?
options: Prominent early sensory loss in a glove-and-stocking distribution
Early sphincter and bladder involvement
Combined upper and lower motor neurone signs without sensory involvement
Symmetrical proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase and myopathic EMG
Ophthalmoplegia with fatigable ptosis
explain: The combination of lower motor neurone signs (wasting, fasciculations of hands and tongue, large-amplitude motor units on EMG) with upper motor neurone signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantars in a wasted limb) and prominent bulbar involvement, in the absence of sensory, sphincter or oculomotor signs, is the hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (motor neurone disease). 🧠 MND is a degeneration of anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts; the striking clinical clue is UMN and LMN signs coexisting in the same region with a pure motor syndrome and normal sensory nerve conduction. Early prominent sensory loss argues against MND and for a peripheral neuropathy. Sphincter involvement is characteristically spared until very late. Symmetrical proximal weakness with raised CK and myopathic EMG points to an inflammatory myopathy. Fatigable ophthalmoplegia and ptosis indicate myasthenia gravis. Riluzole modestly prolongs survival, and non-invasive ventilation improves survival and quality of life; management is multidisciplinary. Diagnosis rests on the revised El Escorial/Awaji criteria.

Early prominent sensory loss argues against MND and for a peripheral neuropathy. Sphincter involvement is characteristically spared until very late. Symmetrical proximal weakness with raised CK and myopathic EMG points to an inflammatory myopathy. Fatigable ophthalmoplegia and ptosis indicate myasthenia gravis. Riluzole modestly prolongs survival, and non-invasive ventilation improves survival and quality of life; management is multidisciplinary. Diagnosis rests on the revised El Escorial/Awaji criteria.

A.html: Motor neurone disease is a pure motor disorder; early glove-and-stocking sensory loss argues strongly against it and points to a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy instead. Normal sensory nerve conduction here confirms sensory sparing.

B.html: Sphincter and bladder function are characteristically preserved until very late in motor neurone disease. Early sphincter involvement should prompt consideration of a spinal cord or cauda equina lesion instead.

C.html: Correct. The coexistence of upper motor neurone signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantars) and lower motor neurone signs (wasting, fasciculations) in a pure motor syndrome with normal sensation is the defining feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (motor neurone disease).

D.html: Symmetrical proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase and myopathic EMG describes an inflammatory myopathy, not motor neurone disease. MND shows neurogenic changes with large-amplitude motor units, not myopathic units.

q: A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while she was straining on the toilet. She describes it as the worst headache of her life, with associated vomiting and neck stiffness. She is now alert with no focal neurological deficit. A non-contrast CT head performed 4 hours after onset is reported as normal. What is the single most appropriate next step in management?
options: Reassure and discharge, as a normal CT within 6 hours excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage
Perform a lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset and analyse CSF for xanthochromia
Arrange an urgent MRI brain with T2-weighted sequences
Start oral sumatriptan and discharge with migraine advice
Immediate CT cerebral angiography alone without further CSF analysis
explain: A thunderclap headache — instantaneous, maximal within seconds, 'worst ever', often on exertion/straining, with vomiting and meningism — demands exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). 🩸 Non-contrast CT is highly sensitive very early: if performed within 6 hours of onset and reported by a competent radiologist, a normal scan makes aneurysmal SAH very unlikely. However, this scan was at 4 hours yet the question tests the classic MRCP teaching that if any doubt remains, or when local protocol requires, a lumbar puncture performed ≥12 hours after headache onset is the confirmatory step. Waiting 12 hours allows red cells to lyse so that bilirubin (xanthochromia), detected by spectrophotometry, forms — distinguishing true SAH from a traumatic tap. Discharging on the basis of a normal early CT alone, without addressing the classic thunderclap presentation, is unsafe in exam terms. MRI is insensitive for acute SAH. Triptans are contraindicated until SAH is excluded. CT angiography identifies aneurysms but does not confirm bleeding and may reveal incidental aneurysms.

q: A 70-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer presents with a 10-day history of progressive mid-thoracic back pain, worse on lying flat and coughing, now with a 2-day history of bilateral leg weakness and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows a spastic paraparesis with a sensory level at T6, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, extensor plantars and a palpable bladder. Which single intervention should be initiated most urgently, before definitive imaging results are available?
options: Immediate high-dose oral dexamethasone with gastric protection
Urgent lumbar puncture to exclude leptomeningeal disease
Empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
Immediate intravenous thrombolysis
Oral gabapentin for neuropathic pain and outpatient MRI
explain: This is metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC): known malignancy, progressive thoracic back pain worse on lying flat and coughing (raised epidural pressure), and an evolving UMN paraparesis with a sensory level and sphincter disturbance. This is a neurological emergency — cord function is time-critical. 🚨 Per NICE guidance (NG202/CG75), once MSCC is suspected clinically, patients should receive high-dose dexamethasone (typically 16 mg daily) with proton-pump-inhibitor cover immediately (unless contraindicated, e.g. suspected lymphoma before diagnosis), while urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours is arranged and definitive treatment (radiotherapy or surgical decompression) is planned. Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic oedema and may temporarily preserve neurological function. Neurological status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome, so delay risks irreversible paraplegia. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated/unhelpful and risks coning. Antibiotics and thrombolysis are irrelevant to a compressive metastatic lesion. Gabapentin with routine outpatient imaging dangerously underestimates the emergency.

q: A 26-year-old woman with obesity presents with a 6-week history of daily headache worse in the morning and on coughing, with transient visual obscurations lasting seconds when she stands, and pulsatile tinnitus. She takes an oral combined contraceptive and recently started a tetracycline for acne. Visual acuity is preserved but there is bilateral papilloedema and an inability to abduct the left eye. CT and MR venography of the brain are normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cmH₂O with normal CSF constituents. Which single explanation best accounts for the failure to abduct the left eye in this condition?
options: Compression of the oculomotor nerve by an enlarging posterior communicating artery aneurysm
A brainstem demyelinating plaque affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Infiltration of the cavernous sinus by granulomatous tissue
A false localising sixth nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure stretching the abducens nerve
Ischaemic mononeuritis of the trochlear nerve due to microvascular disease
explain: The picture — an obese young woman, morning/cough headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, papilloedema, raised opening pressure (34 cmH₂O) with normal CSF and normal imaging/venography — is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Risk is increased by the combined pill and by tetracyclines. 👁️ The inability to abduct the left eye reflects a sixth (abducens) nerve palsy, which in IIH is a classic false localising sign. The abducens nerve has a long intracranial course, bending over the petrous ridge of the temporal bone; raised intracranial pressure stretches or compresses it against the bone, producing a lateral rectus palsy that does not indicate a focal brainstem lesion. This is why it 'falsely localises'. An oculomotor palsy (option A) affects adduction/elevation and pupil, not abduction. An MLF plaque causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Cavernous sinus infiltration would give multiple cranial neuropathies. The trochlear nerve controls the superior oblique, not abduction. Management includes weight loss, acetazolamide, stopping causative drugs, and monitoring vision; refractory cases may need CSF diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration.

B.html: A medial longitudinal fasciculus plaque produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye), not a lateral rectus palsy. The clinical context here is raised intracranial pressure, not demyelination.

C.html: Cavernous sinus pathology typically causes multiple simultaneous cranial neuropathies (III, IV, VI and V1/V2) often with proptosis. An isolated abducens palsy with otherwise normal imaging is better explained by raised intracranial pressure.

D.html: Correct. In raised intracranial pressure, the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve over the petrous ridge makes it vulnerable to stretch, producing a lateral rectus palsy. This is a classic false localising sign and does not indicate a focal brainstem lesion.
